title: The Badger's Lost Property
creature: A badger who runs a lost-property office under a root
summary: Everything left in the wood since 1911, catalogued — and the catalogue is the problem.

chapters.title: Under the Root
chapters.text: The office was under the root of a beech on the boundary bank, and Orla got into it the way everybody gets into these things, which is by losing something and being unreasonable about it. The thing she had lost was a watch. It had been her grandfather's, it had come to her in April when he died, it had not worked since about 2011, and she had worn it every day since the funeral on a strap that was four holes too big. She lost it in the wood on the ninth of October, and she knew exactly where, and it was not there. She knew exactly where because she had felt it go. She had been climbing the bank at the far end by the stile, had put her hand down into the bracken to steady herself, and had felt the strap slide over her knuckles — a sensation so specific that she had stopped and looked at her wrist before she had even finished thinking about it. Four holes too big. She had been meaning to have a hole punched in it since May. She went back twenty times. She took a rake. She took a metal detector belonging to a neighbour, which found two bottle tops and a horseshoe and put her in a very bad mood. On the twelfth visit, in November, in the rain, she was on her hands and knees under the beech on the boundary bank with her arm down a hole between two roots, and something the other end took hold of her sleeve and pulled twice. The hole was not on the bank by the stile. It was two hundred metres away and she had no reason to be at it except that she had by then searched everywhere with a reason and had started on the places without one. She did not scream. She has thought about this since with a certain amount of pride. What she did was take her arm out very slowly and sit back and look at the hole, and the hole looked back at her, and after a moment a badger came about a third of the way out of it and stopped, with its stripes on and its nose going, at a distance of perhaps forty centimetres. It considered her for a while. Then it went back down, and there was a sound like a drawer, and it came up again with something in its mouth and put it on the leaf mould between them. It was a bottle top. It was, she saw when she picked it up, quite an old one — the crimped kind, rusted right through in one place, with a lettering on the top that had gone. Orla, who had had a very frustrating month, said, "That's not mine." The badger looked at the bottle top, and looked at her, and made a noise in its throat that she has never been able to describe and has never mistaken for anything else since, and went back down the hole. She sat under that tree in the rain for another quarter of an hour, and when nothing else happened she went home and did not tell anybody, and came back on the Saturday with a torch and a good deal of nerve.

chapters.title: The Catalogue
chapters.text: The office was not what she expected, and it took her four visits before she was let far enough in to see any of it properly. The entrance under the root opens after about a metre and a half into a chamber that a person can sit up in if they do not mind their hair in the roof. It is dry. That was the first shock: it is completely dry, in a wood, in November, and Orla never worked out how. The second shock was the light. There is some. Not much — enough to see shapes by after your eyes have had four or five minutes — and it does not come from anywhere. There is no gap in the roof; she looked, on three separate visits, with a torch, thoroughly. The light is simply the amount of light there is in that chamber, and it is the same at eleven in the morning and at half past four in December. The things are in the walls. Not piled. Set into the earth in rows, each one pressed into its own small socket, the way you would set eggs into a box, and the rows go round the chamber and back into two passages that Orla was never allowed down. She counted a hundred and seventeen things on her fourth visit before she gave up counting. Counting was hard because the sockets go back into the passages and because she was not allowed to move anything, which was made clear to her early and unmistakably on the third visit when she reached for a key and got a noise she did not need translated. A spectacle case. Four knives. A shoe. A child's shoe and separately a man's boot, not a pair, not near each other. A watch that was not her grandfather's. A brooch. A key with a wooden tag. Six or twelve coins, none of them together. A comb. A thing that turned out, when she got a proper look at it, to be a set of false teeth. And the catalogue. The catalogue is on the floor of the chamber and it is not written and it is not a book. It is marks. There are marks on the packed earth of the floor, hundreds of them, in rows, cut in with a claw and re-cut, and each mark is directly below the socket of the thing it belongs to. Orla could not read it and never learned to. What she learned instead — over about six weeks, by pointing at things and being answered in the only way available, which was that the badger would take a thing out of the wall and turn it and put it back — was what the catalogue was *for*. It was not an inventory. It did not say what the thing was. She established that beyond doubt when she pointed at the false teeth and got shown, in the marks, something nine strokes long. It said what the thing had been doing when it was lost. That sentence took her three weeks to arrive at and about a year to believe, and she would like to set out the evidence, because it sounds like something a child decided and it was not. Two identical objects had different entries. There were two ordinary iron keys in that wall, the same size, the same pattern, almost certainly from the same kind of lock. One had an entry of four strokes. The other had an entry of nine. And one entry served two completely different objects. The comb and one of the coins had the same mark under them — she checked this four times, on different days, from different angles, and once lay flat on the floor with a torch to be sure. Whatever the catalogue was recording, it was not what the things were.

chapters.title: What the Entry Says
chapters.text: Her grandfather's watch was in the wall, third row, near the left-hand passage, and she saw it on the second visit and said so out loud in a voice that came out wrong, and the badger did not give it to her. That was November. She spent from November to March trying to get it. She would like to be clear that the badger never refused her and never drove her off. It did not hide the watch or block the row. On perhaps half her visits it would take the watch out of the wall itself, without being asked, and put it on the floor between them and sit there — and if she reached for it, it would put a paw on it, and that was all, and there was never any question of a struggle. She tried asking. She tried asking politely. She tried explaining, at length, out loud, in a hole in the ground, that it was hers, that it had been her grandfather's, that he had died in April, and that she wanted it back. The badger listened to all of it every time — it always listened, it never once went away while she was talking — and did not give her the watch. In January she brought a photograph of her grandfather, which she now finds embarrassing. In February she got angry and said a number of things she regretted on the walk home. In the first week of March she came in wet and cold and out of ideas and sat down on the floor of the chamber and said, "I don't know what you want." And the badger came over and put one claw on the floor and drew her grandfather's entry, slowly, twice, and then sat back. Orla looked at it for a long time. It was seven strokes. She could not read it. But she had by then spent four months watching that animal draw entries, and she had understood some time in February — without being able to prove it, and without ever telling anybody, because there is no way to say it that does not sound mad — that the entries were not descriptions of objects. Seven strokes was not *a watch*. Seven strokes was whatever the watch had been doing, on the ninth of October, on the wrist of an eleven-year-old girl in a wood. And Orla, sitting on the floor with her back against the earth, realised that she did not know. She knew what the watch was. She did not know what it had been doing. She did not know why it had stopped in 2011 and she did not know why he had gone on wearing it stopped for fourteen years, and she had never asked him, and she was not going to be able to now.

chapters.title: What It Was Doing
chapters.text: She asked her grandmother in the last week of March, in the kitchen at Ballyroe, sitting down, having planned the question for three days and then abandoning the plan entirely and just asking it. Why did he wear a watch that didn't work. Her grandmother put the tea down. She said that it had stopped on the eleventh of June 2011, which was a Saturday, and that they had both been in the car outside the hospital in Galway at the time, and that they had been in that car park for a very long while that afternoon and had not gone in, and that the watch had stopped somewhere in that. She said that he had taken it to be fixed twice and had brought it back both times unfixed, and that on the second occasion the man in Galway had told him it would cost twenty euro and forty minutes, and that he had said no thank you and had walked out. She said that Orla should not make it into more than it was, because he had never once explained himself about it, and that she had asked him exactly twice in fourteen years and had been told, both times, that he was fond of it. Then she said: "But he checked it. That's the thing I'd say if you're wanting a thing to hold. He'd look at it. Two, three times in a day, all those years, he'd turn his wrist over and look at a watch that said twenty past four, and then he'd get on with what he was at." Orla went back to the wood on the second of April. She sat down on the floor of the chamber and she said it out loud, all of it, the whole thing, taking about four minutes and getting it in the wrong order and having to go back twice. The badger listened, the way it always listened. Then it went to the third row near the left-hand passage and took the watch out of the wall and put it on the floor between them, and went back down one of the passages she was never allowed down, and Orla sat there on her own for a while and then went home. She is thirty-four. The watch says twenty past four. She has never had it fixed and has been asked about it perhaps a hundred times, and what she says is that she is fond of it. She has been back to the beech on the boundary bank six or seven times as an adult, and the hole is there, and she has never once put her arm down it, and she thinks about the hundred and five other things in that wall more often than she expected to. Because that is the part that got her, in the end, and it took her until her twenties to see it properly. The catalogue is complete. Every single thing in that wall has an entry, and every entry says what the thing was doing, and the badger has kept all of it dry since 1911. And almost nobody is ever going to come and say it.
